name: French Colonial Empire
summary: France’s second colonial empire, begun with the conquest of Algiers in 1830. It spanned Africa, Indochina and the Pacific, and was second only to Britain’s on the eve of the First World War, before costly wars and decolonisation (1945–1980).

knownFor.label: Francophonie
knownFor.note: French spread as a world language.

location.value: Ruled from Paris over colonies mainly in North and West Africa, Equatorial Africa, Madagascar, Indochina, the Caribbean and the South Pacific. Before the First World War it was the second-largest colonial empire after Britain’s.

terrain.value: From the Sahara and Sahel to tropical forests, Indochina’s river deltas and Pacific islands.
terrain.source: Aldrich, Greater France: A History of French Overseas Expansion (1996)

climate.value: Mostly tropical and arid. Tropical diseases limited European settlement outside Algeria.
climate.source: Aldrich, Greater France: A History of French Overseas Expansion (1996)

resources.value: Colonies supplied raw materials (groundnuts, cotton, rubber, rice, phosphates, wine) and bought French manufactured goods.

disasters.value: Famines and epidemics in colonies, sometimes worsened by forced labour and requisitions. Not detailed in the sources checked.

population.value: By 1870 the second empire covered about 1 million km² with over 5 million inhabitants. It grew greatly after 1880. Today’s overseas territories hold 2.8 million people (2021).

urbanisation.value: Colonial cities grew: Algiers, Dakar, Saigon, Hanoi, Tunis and Casablanca.
urbanisation.source: Aldrich, Greater France: A History of French Overseas Expansion (1996)

disease.value: Colonial medicine (Pasteur Institutes) fought tropical diseases, while forced labour projects caused high death rates.
disease.source: Aldrich, Greater France: A History of French Overseas Expansion (1996)

migration.value: France sent few settlers to most colonies, with the notable exception of Algeria. Colonial soldiers and workers came to France in both World Wars.

economicBase.value: Plantations, mining, cash crops and monocultures serving French industry, often using forced labour.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade between France and its colonies, protected by tariffs (imperial preference).
tradeRoutes.source: Aldrich, Greater France: A History of French Overseas Expansion (1996)

wealth.value: No GDP estimate is given in the sources checked.

moneyAndTax.value: The French franc and colonial currencies (e.g. the CFA franc from 1945). Head taxes and forced labour were imposed on colonial subjects.

inequality.value: Colonial subjects were governed under unequal legal systems and only rarely granted full citizenship. Only a few thousand Algerian Muslims became citizens between 1830 and 1946.

governmentType.value: Colonies, protectorates and mandates ruled from Paris by governors-general. From 1946 to 1958 it was reorganised as the French Union.

keyRulers.value: Charles X (Algiers, 1830). Napoleon III. Jules Ferry (champion of expansion, 1880s). Charles de Gaulle (Free France and decolonisation).

succession.value: Controlled by successive French governments: monarchy, Second Empire, and the Third, Fourth and Fifth Republics.

institutions.value: Governors-general, the indigénat legal code for subjects, and the French Union (1946). Slavery was abolished in French colonies in 1848.

stability.value: Resistance and revolts: Abd al-Qadir in Algeria, the Mokrani Revolt (1871), the Rif War (1921–26), the Madagascar uprising (1947), the Indochina War (1946–54) and the Algerian War (1954–62).

eliteConflict.value: Debate in France between supporters of the “civilising mission” (Jules Ferry) and critics of assimilation.

armyAndTech.value: The French army and Foreign Legion, and colonial troops (e.g. the Senegalese tirailleurs), who also fought in both World Wars.

majorWars.value: The conquest of Algeria (1830–1903). Expansion into Tunisia (1881) and Indochina (1883–93). The Fashoda Incident (1898). The First Indochina War (defeat at Dien Bien Phu, 1954). The Algerian War (1954–62).

territoryChange.value: Rebuilt mostly after 1850. Gained mandates over Syria, Lebanon, Togo and Cameroon after WWI. Lost Indochina (1954) and Algeria (1962). Most African colonies became independent in 1960.

alliancesRivals.value: Rival: Britain (Fashoda, 1898), later an ally (Entente Cordiale, 1904). Rival: Germany (Morocco crises).

inventions.value: Railways, ports and the Suez Canal (built by a French company, 1869). Colonial medicine (Pasteur Institutes).
inventions.source: Aldrich, Greater France: A History of French Overseas Expansion (1996)

scienceEducation.value: French-language schools for a small colonial elite, many of whom later led independence movements.
scienceEducation.source: Aldrich, Greater France: A History of French Overseas Expansion (1996)

openness.value: An official ideology of assimilation (the “mission civilisatrice”), contested in practice by unequal law and racism.

communicationTransport.value: Steamships, the Dakar–Niger railway and other colonial railways built with forced labour in some colonies.

religion.value: Catholic missions in Africa and Indochina. Islam remained majority in North and West Africa.
religion.source: Aldrich, Greater France: A History of French Overseas Expansion (1996)

languageWriting.value: French was spread as the language of administration and education. Today it is the basis of the Francophonie.

artsArchitecture.value: Colonial architecture in Hanoi, Saigon and Dakar. The colonial exhibitions in Paris (1931).
artsArchitecture.source: Aldrich, Greater France: A History of French Overseas Expansion (1996)

socialStructure.value: French citizens versus “French subjects” (until 1946), with settlers, local elites and colonial labourers.

sharedIdentity.value: “Greater France” (la plus grande France), promoted from Paris, while colonised peoples developed their own national movements.
sharedIdentity.source: Aldrich, Greater France: A History of French Overseas Expansion (1996)

dailyLife.value: Colonists lived in European quarters; most colonised people kept local housing and food.

neighbours.value: The British Empire, Germany, Italy, Spain, Siam and Qing China (at its colonial borders).

ideasReligions.value: Spread the French language and republican ideas, which colonised elites used to demand rights and independence.
ideasReligions.source: Aldrich, Greater France: A History of French Overseas Expansion (1996)

colonisation.value: A major coloniser. The conquest of Algeria was very violent, with land dispossession and an estimated 500,000–1,000,000 Algerian deaths (summarised from the article).

riseSignals.value: The conquest of Algiers (1830) and a desire to rebuild prestige after defeat in the Franco-Prussian War (1871), plus economic and “civilising mission” motives.

declineSignals.value: The Second World War and Vichy rule, the refusal of self-government, independence movements, and costly wars in Indochina and Algeria.

outcome.value: Decolonisation. Revolts in Indochina and Algeria “proved costly and France lost both colonies”. Elsewhere decolonisation after 1960 was relatively peaceful. The last colony, Vanuatu, became independent in 1980. Some territories remain French.

sources.value: French colonial archives, and colonial and anti-colonial writings. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026 (only the opening part was read word for word). See also Aldrich (1996).

overallCertainty.value: Good for dates. Death tolls in colonial conquests and wars (e.g. Algeria) are debated. Dates vary (e.g. the Algerian conquest “completed” in 1852, 1903 or 1920). Second source: Wikidata starts the first French colonial empire in 1534; this app’s entry covers the second empire from 1830.
